responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn parasomnia research unit faces inherent tensions between ecological validity and experimental control, participant safety and data richness, and throughput volume versus annotation quality. These levers address these conflicts by modulating the intensity of monitoring, the breadth of recruitment, and the depth of data analysis. Balancing these factors is crucial for generating robust, generalizable findings while maintaining ethical standards and operational feasibility.

levers.name: PSG Escalation Threshold
levers.consequences: Lowering the threshold for full PSG escalation captures more events at clinical-grade resolution, but increases technician workload and participant burden. Raising the threshold reduces burden, but risks missing subtle or atypical events, biasing the dataset towards severe episodes.
options: Escalate to full PSG only after two independent technician flags within a single night
Trigger full PSG based on a single technician flag plus algorithm-detected anomaly
Deploy full PSG immediately upon any technician-flagged event
levers.review_lever: Escalating to full PSG on any technician flag maximizes data capture but may overwhelm resources and reduce technician vigilance over time.

levers.name: Exclusion Criteria Stringency
levers.consequences: Stricter exclusion criteria improve data homogeneity and reduce confounding factors, but limit recruitment pool and generalizability. Looser criteria expand recruitment, but increase the risk of including participants with comorbid conditions that obscure parasomnia-specific mechanisms.
options: Exclude all participants with any history of psychiatric comorbidity, regardless of current stability
Allow participants with stable, treated psychiatric conditions, assessed by the study psychologist
Enroll participants with mild, untreated anxiety or depression, but stratify by these factors in analysis
levers.review_lever: Excluding all psychiatric comorbidities ensures a cleaner sample but may not reflect the real-world prevalence of parasomnias.

levers.name: Sensor Modality Prioritization
levers.consequences: Prioritizing high-resolution sensor modalities (e.g., full PSG) increases data richness for captured events, but reduces the number of participants that can be monitored simultaneously due to technician workload. Prioritizing low-burden modalities (e.g., dry-EEG) enables higher throughput, but sacrifices detailed physiological characterization.
options: Focus primarily on high-density EEG and EMG data, limiting participant slots to 6 initially
Emphasize contact-free mattress sensors and infrared video, expanding to the full 8 slots
Balance EEG and contact-free data, using 7 participant slots to optimize data breadth
levers.review_lever: Focusing on high-density EEG limits throughput but provides richer data for characterizing parasomnia subtypes.

levers.name: Control Group Matching Rigor
levers.consequences: Tighter matching criteria for the control group (e.g., age, sex, BMI, sleep hygiene) strengthens the validity of between-group comparisons, but makes recruitment more difficult and time-consuming. Looser matching accelerates recruitment, but increases the risk of confounding variables influencing the benchmarked event-triage model.
options: Match controls strictly on age, sex, and BMI, accepting a slower recruitment rate
Match controls on age and sex only, prioritizing recruitment speed and sample size
Use a propensity score matching approach, weighting multiple factors to optimize balance
levers.review_lever: Strict control group matching improves statistical power but may significantly slow down the recruitment process.

levers.name: Annotation Pipeline Depth
levers.consequences: More detailed annotation protocols (e.g., micro-arousal scoring, respiratory event analysis) increase the richness of the dataset and the potential for novel findings, but require more technician time and scoring resources. Simpler protocols reduce annotation burden, but may miss subtle features relevant to parasomnia pathophysiology.
options: Implement detailed micro-arousal and respiratory event scoring, increasing annotation time per event
Focus solely on AASM-defined macro-arousals and motor events, streamlining the annotation process
Use a hybrid approach, scoring micro-arousals only during full-PSG escalation nights
levers.review_lever: Detailed annotation protocols increase data richness but strain resources, potentially delaying publication timelines.

levers.name: Episode Capture Window
levers.consequences: Extending the maximum participant stay increases the probability of capturing infrequent parasomnia events, but also increases per-participant costs and the risk of participant attrition. Shortening the stay reduces costs, but may result in an underestimation of episode frequency and severity.
options: Cap participant stays at a maximum of 6 weeks, regardless of event capture
Extend stays up to 12 weeks for participants with fewer than two captured events
Offer a 'booster' weekend stay after initial discharge for participants with suspected events
levers.review_lever: Longer participant stays increase the likelihood of capturing events but also raise costs and attrition risks.

levers.name: Data Sharing Scope
levers.consequences: Broader data sharing (e.g., including limited video excerpts with explicit consent) increases the impact and reproducibility of the research, but raises privacy concerns and requires more extensive ethics review. Restricting data sharing to physiological signals reduces privacy risks, but limits the utility of the dataset for external researchers.
options: Share only de-identified physiological data and summary statistics, minimizing privacy risks
Share limited video excerpts of motor events with explicit participant consent and blurring
Create a secure, on-site data enclave for external researchers to access sensitive data
levers.review_lever: Sharing video excerpts enhances data utility but necessitates stringent privacy protocols and participant consent procedures.

responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn sleep research unit faces inherent tensions between ecological validity and experimental control, participant safety and data richness, and manual annotation effort and throughput. The selected levers address these conflicts directly. 'Environmental Enrichment Protocol' balances naturalistic behavior with controlled stimuli. 'Technician Training Curriculum' mitigates false alarms while maximizing event capture. 'Data Retention Horizon' balances immediate analysis needs with long-term research potential, and 'Control Group Diversity' balances statistical power with generalizability.

levers.name: Environmental Enrichment Protocol
levers.consequences: Introducing controlled stimuli (e.g., ambient noise, light levels) may trigger or exacerbate parasomnia episodes, increasing event capture rates. However, this risks altering the naturalistic sleep environment, potentially skewing baseline behavior and reducing generalizability to real-world settings.
options: Maintain a strictly neutral, home-like environment to minimize external influence on sleep patterns.
Introduce subtle, pre-approved environmental manipulations to provoke parasomnia events under controlled conditions.
Personalize the sleep environment based on participant preference to promote relaxation and natural sleep.
levers.review_lever: Stimulus-driven provocation may bias the observed parasomnia phenotypes, limiting the study's ability to characterize spontaneous, naturally occurring events.

levers.name: Technician Training Curriculum
levers.consequences: Comprehensive training in parasomnia recognition and emergency response improves data quality and participant safety. However, extensive training increases personnel costs and may lead to technician fatigue, potentially reducing vigilance during overnight shifts.
options: Prioritize rapid response and safety protocols to minimize immediate risks during parasomnia events.
Emphasize subtle parasomnia event recognition to maximize the capture of nuanced behavioral phenomena.
Balance safety and recognition training to ensure both participant well-being and comprehensive data collection.
levers.review_lever: Over-emphasis on rare, dramatic events may desensitize technicians to more subtle, but equally informative, parasomnia manifestations.

levers.name: Data Retention Horizon
levers.consequences: Longer data retention allows for future re-analysis and exploration of novel research questions. However, extended storage increases costs and necessitates robust data security measures to protect participant privacy, especially given the video component.
options: Retain data for the minimum duration required by funding agencies to minimize storage costs and security risks.
Archive data indefinitely for potential future research, contingent on ongoing funding for storage and security.
Establish a rolling retention policy, purging data after a set period unless a specific research need is identified.
levers.review_lever: Indefinite retention, while maximizing future research options, creates a growing liability regarding data security and evolving ethical standards.

levers.name: Control Group Diversity
levers.consequences: A more diverse control group enhances the generalizability of findings to the broader population. However, recruiting a highly diverse control group increases recruitment costs and may introduce confounding variables that complicate data analysis.
options: Recruit a narrowly defined control group matched on key demographics to minimize confounding variables.
Target a highly diverse control group reflecting the broader population to maximize the generalizability of findings.
Stratify the control group by demographic factors to allow for subgroup analysis and control of confounding variables.
levers.review_lever: A highly homogenous control group, while simplifying analysis, may limit the applicability of the event-triage model to diverse patient populations.

levers.name: PSG Montage Density
levers.consequences: Higher-density PSG montages capture more detailed neurophysiological data, potentially revealing subtle biomarkers. However, increased electrode count raises setup time, participant discomfort, and annotation complexity, potentially reducing compliance and throughput.
options: Employ a minimalist PSG montage focusing on essential channels to maximize participant comfort and throughput.
Utilize a high-density PSG montage to capture detailed neurophysiological data for in-depth analysis.
Adapt the PSG montage based on individual participant characteristics and research questions to balance data richness and feasibility.
levers.review_lever: Overly complex montages may introduce artifact and noise that obscure genuine physiological signals, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio.

levers.name: Episode Trigger Definition
levers.consequences: A broad definition captures more potential parasomnia events, increasing statistical power. However, it also increases the number of false positives requiring manual review, potentially overwhelming annotation resources and reducing precision.
options: Define parasomnia episodes narrowly to minimize false positives and focus annotation efforts on high-confidence events.
Define parasomnia episodes broadly to maximize event capture and ensure comprehensive coverage of potential phenomena.
Employ a tiered definition, categorizing events by probability to prioritize annotation efforts based on confidence level.
levers.review_lever: An overly restrictive definition risks missing subtle or atypical parasomnia events, leading to an incomplete characterization of the phenomenon.

responses.strategic_rationale: This project faces a core tension between ecological validity and experimental control. The desire to capture naturalistic parasomnia events in a home-like setting conflicts with the need for rigorous physiological monitoring and participant safety. The levers below address this tension by modulating the intensity of monitoring, the breadth of the participant pool, and the balance between manual and automated analysis, all while considering the budget and timeline constraints.

levers.name: Enhanced Night Cadence
levers.consequences: Increasing enhanced-night PSG frequency improves physiological data granularity and confidence in event characterization. However, more frequent PSG nights increase technician workload, participant burden, and scoring costs, potentially reducing overall study throughput and increasing participant dropout.
options: Schedule enhanced PSG nights weekly to capture more frequent physiological data.
Trigger enhanced PSG nights only after a technician-flagged event to minimize burden.
Implement enhanced PSG on nights 1, 3, and 5 to balance data capture and participant comfort.
levers.review_lever: Increasing PSG frequency may not proportionally increase novel findings if the core parasomnia events are already well-characterized by the lower-resolution sensors.

levers.name: Exclusion Criteria Breadth

options: Relax exclusion criteria to include participants with well-controlled OSA.
Maintain strict exclusion criteria to ensure a homogeneous parasomnia cohort.
Implement staged inclusion, enrolling complex cases after the core cohort is established.
levers.review_lever: Relaxing exclusion criteria without a clear stratification strategy risks diluting the core parasomnia signal with noise from comorbid conditions.

levers.name: Sensor Stream Redundancy
levers.consequences: Increasing sensor redundancy (e.g., multiple EEG channels, overlapping camera views) improves data robustness and allows for cross-validation of event detection. options: Prioritize fewer, higher-quality sensor streams to reduce data processing overhead.
Implement overlapping sensor streams to ensure data integrity and cross-validation.
Focus on a single, validated sensor stream to minimize data complexity and cost.
levers.review_lever: Redundant sensor streams may yield diminishing returns if the primary sensors already provide sufficient signal fidelity for event detection.

levers.name: Annotation Team Size
levers.consequences: Increasing the annotation team size accelerates data throughput and reduces the backlog of unannotated data. However, it also increases personnel costs and the complexity of managing inter-rater reliability, potentially introducing systematic biases.
options: Maintain a small, highly trained annotation team to ensure consistency.
Expand the annotation team to accelerate data throughput and reduce backlogs.
Outsource initial annotation to a third party to reduce internal workload.
levers.review_lever: Expanding the annotation team without a robust inter-rater reliability protocol could introduce more noise than signal into the adjudicated event dataset.

levers.name: Episode Morphology Granularity

options: Focus on coarse episode characterization to maximize annotation throughput.
Prioritize detailed episode characterization to enable fine-grained phenotyping.
Implement a tiered annotation approach, starting with coarse features and escalating to detailed analysis.
levers.review_lever: Overly granular episode characterization may lead to overfitting the phenotyping model, reducing its generalizability to new datasets.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off. Be concise and grounded — only cite numbers the project context provides directly. Target length: 30–60 words.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A one-sentence critical review (20–40 words). Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO fabricated statistics or percentages without evidence from the project context
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to 20–40 words.
   - Each option: 15–25 words, a concrete actionable approach with an action verb.
   - Maintain parallel grammatical structure across options
   - Ensure options are self-contained descriptions
user_prompt:
File 'plan.txt':
Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
